correctness.rationale: An exact vertex-component argument proves F_1=s, F_2=2s[1+p(1-s)] and the triangle F_3 formula; their difference is ps(1-s)[2+6p-6p²-ps(9-6p)]. Under 0<p,s<1 the prefactor is positive and A-B=2-3p gives the sharp classification and all ties. The derivative of the crossover curve is strictly negative. For size-two households the gap is 2ps(1-s)>0, proving minimality. The standalone enumerator checks all configurations and 2533 exact rational assertions, not an infinite-range substitute for algebra.

originality.rationale: All six exact semantic comparisons were carried out against published mathematical findings, with the nearest household/epidemic items concerned instead with reproduction-number rankings, transmission laws or continuous-time differential equations. Relevant original published works were inspected where accessible, notably 2012 Keeling–Shattock, 2004 Ball–Britton–Lyne, 2014/2015 Yuan et al. and 2017 Ball–Sirl. None of the inspected main proofs establishes or dominates the exact two-identical-triangle, two-dose, independent-seed phase boundary. Model architecture and broad concentration phenomena are recognized prior work. The unavailable 2002 Ball–Lyne full text creates a stated residual priority risk.
residual_risks: The 2002 Ball–Lyne article has a highly relevant household vaccination title and its complete original text was inaccessible after open-source attempts and institutional-access attempt; its abstract indicates a reproduction-threshold objective but a finite example cannot be excluded.
Some old household optimization or Reed–Frost/percolation papers could imply this six-person special case without using these exact keywords.
No independent priority assessment has been performed.

value.rationale: The fixed two-dose decision between *identical* three-person households is the first nondegenerate equal-household design with a genuine possible benefit of concentrating both doses, unlike the two-person case. Resolving its exact p–s threshold, the unique crossover, and all ties clarifies how independently introduced infections and small-household contact reliability jointly control a natural intervention objective. This is a complete finite mathematical benchmark, not a numerical slice or a new general vaccination principle; practical conclusions require a richer model.
